title: Consumer groups, rebalancing and lag
summary: How partitions are shared inside a group, eager versus cooperative rebalancing and the new KIP-848 protocol, committed offsets, auto.offset.reset and reading lag like an on-call engineer.

steps.title: A group shares the partitions
body: Consumers that use the same `group.id` form a **consumer group**. Kafka gives every partition of the subscribed
topics to **exactly one** member of the group. Different groups are independent: each gets every record.
```text
topic orders:   P0  P1  P2  P3  P4  P5
group "billing" (3 members)                 group "analytics" (1 member)
billing-1  <- P0 P1                          analytics-1 <- P0 P1 P2 P3 P4 P5
billing-2  <- P2 P3
billing-3  <- P4 P5
billing-4  <- (nothing: more members than partitions is idle capacity)
committed offsets live in __consumer_offsets, per (group, topic, partition):
billing   orders-3 -> 41877        analytics orders-3 -> 90100
- The **partition count caps the parallelism** of a group: a 7th consumer on a 6-partition topic sits idle.
- Two deployments of the same service that accidentally use **different** `group.id`s each process every record
(two emails to every customer). Two different services that share one `group.id` split the records between them
(each misses half).
- Under the **classic** protocol the members agree on an assignment through a client-side **assignor**: `range`
(per topic, contiguous ranges, sorted by member id), `roundrobin`, or `cooperative-sticky`.
> **See it:** in **Labs → Messaging builder → Kafka**, play *More consumers than partitions* and *Two groups, two emails*.

steps.title: The range assignor
prompt: Write `Dictionary<string, List<int>> RangeAssign(List<string> members, int partitions)` for one topic.
- Sort the members by name (ordinal).
- Each member gets `partitions / n` consecutive partitions; the first `partitions % n` members (in sorted order) get
one extra.
- Every member appears in the result, members with nothing get an empty list. No members → an empty dictionary.
Example: members `c2, c1, c3` and 7 partitions → `c1: 0,1,2`, `c2: 3,4`, `c3: 5,6`.
starter: Dictionary<string, List<int>> RangeAssign(List<string> members, int partitions)

int per = partitions / sorted.Count, extra = partitions % sorted.Count, next = 0;
hints: `per = partitions / n`, `extra = partitions % n`; member `i` gets `per + (i < extra ? 1 : 0)`.

steps.title: Rebalancing: eager, cooperative and KIP-848
body: A **rebalance** happens when a member joins, leaves, crashes (no heartbeat within `session.timeout.ms`, 45 s
default) or stops polling (more than `max.poll.interval.ms`, 5 min default, between `Consume` calls).
| Protocol | What happens on a rebalance |
| classic, **eager** (`range`, `roundrobin`) | **every** member revokes **all** its partitions, the group stops, then gets a new assignment: a stop-the-world pause on every join or leave |

| classic, **cooperative-sticky** | members keep the partitions that do not move; only the moved ones are revoked, in a second round. Set `PartitionAssignmentStrategy = PartitionAssignmentStrategy.CooperativeSticky` |

| **consumer** protocol (KIP-848, GA in Kafka 4.0) | the **broker** computes the assignment and hands out changes in heartbeats; no group-wide barrier, members are not paused. Client side: `group.protocol=consumer` (librdkafka 2.10+: `cc.Set("group.protocol", "consumer")`); client-side assignor settings no longer apply |
**Static membership** (`GroupInstanceId = "billing-" + podName`) lets a restarted pod come back with its old
partitions without a rebalance, as long as it returns within `session.timeout.ms`. Rolling deploys of a big
group stop shuffling partitions around.
Handle revocations: in Confluent.Kafka use `SetPartitionsRevokedHandler` / `SetPartitionsLostHandler` to commit or
stop work for the partitions you are losing.

steps.prompt: A 3-member billing group on 12 partitions uses the **classic eager** protocol. A 4th member joins during a deploy. What do the three existing members experience?
options: All three revoke all 12 partitions and pause until the new assignment, although only 3 partitions actually move
Nothing: only the 3 partitions that move are paused
The new member waits until the next restart of the group
The broker moves partitions without telling the consumers
explain: That stop-the-world pause on every join and leave is why `cooperative-sticky` and then the broker-side consumer
protocol (KIP-848) exist. With cooperative-sticky, the three members keep 9 partitions and keep processing, and only
3 are revoked and handed to the new member.

steps.title: A sticky group that rebalances on join and leave
prompt: Write a class `ConsumerGroup` that keeps assignments **sticky**, the way `cooperative-sticky` does.
- `ConsumerGroup(int partitions)`; partitions are `0..partitions-1`.
- `void Join(string member)` and `void Leave(string member)`: change the membership and run a rebalance.
- `List<int> Owned(string member)`: its partitions, ascending (empty for unknown members).
- `int Generation`: how many rebalances have run.
- `List<int> LastRevoked`: ascending, the partitions the last rebalance **took away from members that stayed** in
the group (partitions of a member that left are not revocations).
Rebalance rule (members sorted by name, ordinal):
1. target per member = `partitions / n`, plus one for the first `partitions % n` members;
2. each member keeps its current partitions, lowest first, up to its target; the rest are revoked;
3. the partitions nobody owns now are handed out in ascending order to members below target, member by member in
sorted order.
With 6 partitions: `a` joins → a owns 0-5. `b` joins → a keeps 0,1,2 and 3,4,5 are revoked and go to b. An eager
rebalance would have revoked all 6.
solution: public int Generation { get; private set; }
public List<int> LastRevoked { get; private set; } = new();
owned.TryGetValue(member, out var p) ? p.OrderBy(x => x).ToList() : new List<int>();
int per = partitions / members.Count, extra = partitions % members.Count;
hints: Keep a `SortedDictionary<string, List<int>>` with an ordinal comparer: member order is then the sorted order.
First pass: keep `mine.Take(target)`, revoke `mine.Skip(target)`. Second pass: hand out the free partitions from a `Queue<int>`.
Do not count the partitions of the member that left as revoked: it is no longer in the dictionary when you rebalance.

Dojo.Eq("b joins: a keeps 0,1,2", new List<int> { 0, 1, 2 }, dojoG.Owned("a"));
Dojo.Eq("only the moved partitions were revoked", new List<int> { 3, 4, 5 }, dojoG.LastRevoked);
Dojo.Eq("c joins: only 2 and 5 move", new List<int> { 2, 5 }, dojoG.LastRevoked);
Dojo.Eq("c owns 2 and 5", new List<int> { 2, 5 }, dojoG.Owned("c"));
Dojo.Eq("b keeps 3 and 4", new List<int> { 3, 4 }, dojoG.Owned("b"));
Dojo.Eq("b leaves: nothing is revoked from a or c", new List<int>(), dojoG.LastRevoked);
Dojo.Eq("a picks up 3", new List<int> { 0, 1, 3 }, dojoG.Owned("a"));
Dojo.Eq("c picks up 4", new List<int> { 2, 4, 5 }, dojoG.Owned("c"));

steps.title: Committed offsets, lag and auto.offset.reset
body: The **committed offset** of a group for a partition is the **next** offset it will read. So:
```text
^ committed (CURRENT-OFFSET) 41877
LAG = 90512 - 41877 = 48635 records not yet processed
**Commit after processing**, never before: in Confluent.Kafka set `EnableAutoOffsetStore = false` and call
`consumer.StoreOffset(cr)` after the handler succeeded (the background auto-commit then commits only stored offsets),
or turn auto-commit off and call `consumer.Commit(cr)`. Committing first loses the record if you crash in between
(*Committed, then crashed*); committing after gives at-least-once, so make the handler idempotent.
**`auto.offset.reset`** applies when the group has **no valid committed offset** for a partition: a brand-new group,
or a committed offset that retention has deleted (below the log start offset):
| Value | Starts at | Use it for |
| `latest` (default) | the log end: only new records | caches, notifications that are useless when old |
| `earliest` | the log start: everything still stored | anything that must not miss data: billing, projections |
| `none` | throws an error | when a silent jump must page a human |
Committed offsets of a group are deleted after `offsets.retention.minutes` (7 days) once the group is **empty**,
so a consumer that was switched off for two weeks restarts via `auto.offset.reset`, too.
> **See it:** in **Labs → Messaging builder → Kafka**, play *Committed, then crashed* and *The new service saw nothing*.

steps.prompt: billing's lag alert fired. You run `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group billing` twice, five minutes apart (second run shown, the first had CURRENT-OFFSET 41877 for partition 3 as well). What is the most likely cause?
code: GROUP    TOPIC   PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG    CONSUMER-ID   HOST         CLIENT-ID
options: The consumer that owns orders-3 is stuck on the record at offset 41877 (a poison record that fails and is retried forever), while the other partitions are fine
Retention deleted the records of partition 3
The group has too many members
explain: Lag on **one** partition with a CURRENT-OFFSET that does **not move** while LOG-END-OFFSET grows means the owner is
not making progress there: the classic poison record (deserialisation error, a handler that always throws) or a
handler blocked on a dependency. The same member owns partition 2 and is fine there because librdkafka fetches per
partition. Lag spread over **all** partitions and growing would instead mean too little consumer capacity.
Fix the handler or send the record to a dead-letter topic. As a last resort skip it: stop the group, then
check the plan, run again with `--execute`. Practise exactly this in **Labs → Live network labs → 25 Live Kafka lab**.

steps.title: Lag and where a consumer starts
prompt: Write the two calculations behind every lag dashboard and every "why did it skip / replay?" question.
- `long? Lag(long logEndOffset, long? committed)`: `logEndOffset - committed`, never below 0; `null` when there is no
committed offset (the CLI prints `-`).
- `long StartOffset(long? committed, long logStart, long logEnd, string autoOffsetReset)`: where the consumer begins
reading a partition.
- A committed offset inside `[logStart, logEnd]` is used as it is.
- Otherwise (none, or out of range) `autoOffsetReset` decides: `"earliest"` → `logStart`, `"latest"` → `logEnd`,
anything else (`"none"`) → throw `InvalidOperationException`.
starter: long StartOffset(long? committed, long logStart, long logEnd, string autoOffsetReset)
solution: long StartOffset(long? committed, long logStart, long logEnd, string autoOffsetReset)
if (committed is long c && c >= logStart && c <= logEnd) return c;
_ => throw new InvalidOperationException("no valid committed offset and auto.offset.reset=none"),
hints: `Lag`: return `null` for a missing commit, otherwise `Math.Max(0, logEndOffset - committed.Value)`.
`StartOffset`: `if (committed is long c && c >= logStart && c <= logEnd) return c;` then a `switch` on the reset policy.
template: Dojo.Eq("lag is log end minus committed", (long?)48635, Lag(90512, 41877));
Dojo.Eq("no committed offset: no lag value", (long?)null, Lag(5300, null));
Dojo.Eq("a valid committed offset wins", 1200L, StartOffset(1200, 1000, 1500, "latest"));
Dojo.Eq("committed exactly at the log end is valid", 1500L, StartOffset(1500, 1000, 1500, "earliest"));
Dojo.Eq("new group + latest: the new service sees nothing old", 1500L, StartOffset(null, 1000, 1500, "latest"));
Dojo.Eq("new group + earliest: everything still stored", 1000L, StartOffset(null, 1000, 1500, "earliest"));
Dojo.Eq("retention deleted the committed offset: earliest jumps to the log start", 1000L, StartOffset(400, 1000, 1500, "earliest"));
Dojo.Eq("retention deleted it and latest skips everything", 1500L, StartOffset(400, 1000, 1500, "latest"));

steps.title: Read the describe output like on-call
prompt: On-call pastes two `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe` outputs taken a few minutes apart. Turn them into findings.
Write `static class LagMonitor` with `public static List<string> Findings(string[] before, string[] after, long minLag)`.
Each data row has the columns `GROUP TOPIC PARTITION CURRENT-OFFSET LOG-END-OFFSET LAG CONSUMER-ID HOST CLIENT-ID`
separated by one or more spaces; skip the header row (it starts with `GROUP`) and blank lines. `CURRENT-OFFSET` and
`LAG` are `-` when the group has no committed offset; `CONSUMER-ID` is `-` when no member owns the partition.
For every row of `after`, in order, add at most one finding (the first rule that applies), named `"{topic}-{partition}"`:
1. no owner and lag > 0 → `"orders-5: no consumer, lag 900"`
2. no committed offset → `"orders-4: no committed offset"`
3. the same partition in `before` had the **same** CURRENT-OFFSET and lag > 0 → `"orders-3: stuck at 41877, lag 48635"`
4. lag grew compared with `before` and is at least `minLag` → `"orders-2: lag growing 1008 -> 2050"`
Finally add `"total lag {sum}"`, the sum of the numeric lags in `after`.
starter: public static List<string> Findings(string[] before, string[] after, long minLag)
solution: record Row(string Topic, int Partition, long? Current, long? Lag, string Consumer);
static long? Num(string s) => s == "-" ? null : long.Parse(s);
.Select(c => new Row(c[1], int.Parse(c[2]), Num(c[3]), Num(c[5]), c[6]))
public static List<string> Findings(string[] before, string[] after, long minLag)
else if (r.Current is null) result.Add($"{name}: no committed offset");
else if (o is not null && o.Current == r.Current && r.Lag > 0) result.Add($"{name}: stuck at {r.Current}, lag {r.Lag}");
